solution: Several examples show microbes releasing gases during their metabolic activity: (i) yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) releases carbon dioxide (CO2) gas during fermentation of sugars to produce alcohol — this CO2 is what causes dough to rise in bread-making; (ii) the puffed appearance of idli/dosa batter is due to CO2 released by fermenting bacteria/yeast present in the batter; (iii) methanogens such as Methanobacterium (present in the rumen of cattle and in biogas plants) release methane gas along with CO2 and hydrogen as they anaerobically break down cellulosic plant material — this methane-rich mixture is used as biogas/gobar gas fuel.
steps: Yeast releases CO2 during alcoholic fermentation — makes bread dough rise
Fermenting batter (idli/dosa) becomes puffy due to CO2 release by microbes
Methanogenic bacteria (e.g., Methanobacterium) in cattle rumen/biogas plants release methane gas from cellulose breakdown
These are clear evidence of gas release as a metabolic product of microbes

question: In which food would you find lactic acid bacteria? Mention some of their useful applications.
solution: Lactic acid bacteria (LAB), such as Lactobacillus, are found in milk and milk products, especially in curd (dahi)/yogurt. Applications: (i) they convert milk to curd by producing lactic acid, which coagulates and partially digests milk proteins, and significantly increases the vitamin B12 content of curd; (ii) they play a beneficial role in the human gut/stomach, checking disease-causing microbes; (iii) LAB and other microorganisms are also involved in the fermentation of batters for idli, dosa and other foods, producing carbon dioxide and lactic acid that make the food porous and improve flavour and digestibility; and (iv) commercially, LAB is used in the dairy industry to prepare a variety of fermented milk products.
steps: Lactic acid bacteria are found in milk and its products, especially curd
They convert milk to curd, increasing its vitamin B12 content
They check disease-causing microbes in the human gut when consumed
Also used in fermentation of idli/dosa batters and other fermented foods

question: Name some traditional Indian foods made of wheat, rice and Bengal gram (or their products) which involve use of microbes.
solution: Traditional Indian fermented foods made using microbes include: from rice/rice-urad dal batter — idli and dosa (fermented using bacteria and yeasts present in the batter, giving them their characteristic puffiness and flavour); from wheat — bread (leavened using yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae); and from Bengal gram (chickpea flour/besan) — foods like dhokla, which are prepared by fermentation using yeast/bacteria present in the batter.
steps: Rice + urad dal batter fermented by bacteria/yeast -> idli, dosa
Wheat dough leavened by yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) -> bread
Bengal gram (besan) batter fermented by yeast/bacteria -> dhokla

question: In which way have microbes played a major role in controlling diseases caused by harmful bacteria?
solution: Microbes have played a major role in controlling bacterial diseases through the discovery and production of antibiotics — chemical substances produced by certain microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) that can kill or inhibit the growth of other, disease-causing microorganisms. For example, the fungus Penicillium notatum produces penicillin, which was the first antibiotic to be discovered (by Alexander Fleming) and has saved millions of lives from bacterial infections. Various other microbes similarly produce antibiotics that are commercially mass-produced (using industrial fermentation technology) and used extensively in medicine to treat bacterial infections such as pneumonia, tuberculosis and many others, dramatically reducing mortality from these diseases.
steps: Certain microbes (bacteria/fungi) naturally produce antibiotics that kill or inhibit other harmful bacteria
Penicillium notatum produces penicillin, discovered by Alexander Fleming — the first antibiotic
Antibiotics are commercially mass-produced through microbial fermentation
Their use in medicine has drastically reduced mortality from bacterial infectious diseases

question: Name any two species of fungus, which are used in the production of the antibiotics.
solution: Two examples of fungi used in antibiotic production are: (i) Penicillium notatum (and Penicillium chrysogenum), which produce the antibiotic Penicillin; and (ii) Cephalosporium species, which produce the antibiotic Cephalosporin.
steps: Penicillium notatum/chrysogenum produce penicillin
Cephalosporium species produce cephalosporin

question: What is sewage? In which way can sewage be harmful to us?
solution: Sewage refers to the municipal waste water, which mostly consists of used/waste water released from households, along with waste from other sources (industries, etc.), containing large amounts of organic matter and microbes (many of which are pathogenic). Sewage is harmful because it contains a large number of disease-causing microorganisms (pathogens) that can contaminate drinking-water sources and cause serious water-borne diseases like cholera, typhoid, dysentery and hepatitis if released into water bodies without treatment. Additionally, if discharged untreated into rivers/water bodies, it consumes a large amount of dissolved oxygen (high Biochemical Oxygen Demand) as aerobic microbes decompose the organic matter present in it, thereby depleting oxygen levels and harming aquatic organisms like fish.
steps: Sewage = municipal waste water, largely from households, rich in organic matter and microbes
Contains numerous pathogenic microorganisms that can cause water-borne diseases if untreated
Has high organic content, so it has a high Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD)
Untreated discharge depletes dissolved oxygen in water bodies, killing aquatic life

question: What is the key difference between primary and secondary sewage treatment?
solution: Primary sewage treatment involves physical removal of particles from sewage through sequential filtration and sedimentation — removing floating debris by sequential filtration, and removal of grit (soil, small pebbles) by sedimentation; all solids that settle form the primary sludge, while the supernatant liquid (effluent) is taken for secondary treatment. Secondary (biological) treatment involves passing the primary effluent into large aeration tanks, where it is constantly agitated mechanically and air is pumped in, allowing aerobic microbes to grow abundantly as flocs and consume the major part of the organic matter present, thereby significantly reducing the BOD of the effluent, followed by settling of the microbial floc (activated sludge) before the clarified effluent is released. Thus, primary treatment is a purely physical process to remove solids, while secondary treatment is a biological process using microbes to break down and reduce the dissolved/suspended organic pollutant load.
steps: Primary treatment: physical removal of solids via filtration and sedimentation (produces primary sludge)
Secondary treatment: biological process — aerobic microbes in aeration tanks consume organic matter, reducing BOD
Key difference: primary is physical removal of solids; secondary is microbial/biological degradation of dissolved organic matter

question: Do you think microbes can also be used as source of energy? If yes, how?
solution: Yes, microbes can be used as a source of energy. Certain methanogenic bacteria, such as Methanobacterium, grow anaerobically on cellulosic material and produce a large amount of methane along with carbon dioxide and hydrogen. This mixture of gases is called biogas (or gobar gas), which is combustible and used as a fuel for cooking and lighting. Biogas plants use cattle dung (rich in cellulosic waste and inoculated with these bacteria present in the rumen of cattle) as raw material in an anaerobic digester, producing biogas as a renewable and eco-friendly source of energy, along with the slurry left behind being useful as manure.
steps: Yes — methanogenic bacteria (e.g., Methanobacterium) produce methane-rich biogas from cellulosic waste
Biogas plants use cattle dung slurry in anaerobic digesters as raw material
Biogas (methane + CO2 + H2) is combustible and used as fuel for cooking/lighting
Leftover slurry can also be used as organic manure

question: Microbes can be used to decrease the use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides. Explain how this can be accomplished.
solution: Microbes can replace/reduce dependence on chemical fertilisers and pesticides through: (i) Biofertilisers — organisms that enrich soil nutrients, e.g., nitrogen-fixing bacteria like Rhizobium (in symbiotic association with legume roots) and free-living forms like Azospirillum and Azotobacter, which fix atmospheric nitrogen into the soil, reducing the need for chemical nitrogenous fertilisers; blue-green algae/cyanobacteria (e.g., Nostoc, Anabaena) that also fix nitrogen and add organic matter to enrich paddy field soil; and fungi forming mycorrhizal associations with plant roots (e.g., Glomus), which help absorb phosphorus from soil. (ii) Biopesticides/biological control agents — organisms that control pests and pathogens without chemical pesticides, e.g., Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), whose toxin protein controls insect larvae/pests (used in Bt crops and Bt-based biopesticide sprays), Trichoderma species that act as biocontrol agents against several plant pathogens, and the use of the baculovirus Nucleopolyhedrovirus, a very species-specific and eco-friendly biological control agent for insect pests, particularly suited for use in Integrated Pest Management (IPM) programmes.
steps: Biofertilisers: Rhizobium, Azospirillum, Azotobacter fix atmospheric nitrogen, reducing need for chemical N-fertiliser
Cyanobacteria (Nostoc, Anabaena) fix nitrogen and enrich paddy soils; mycorrhizal fungi (Glomus) aid phosphorus uptake
Biopesticides: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) toxin controls insect pests without chemical pesticides
Biocontrol agents like Trichoderma (against plant pathogens) and baculoviruses (species-specific insect control) reduce pesticide use

question: Three water samples namely river water, untreated sewage water and secondary effluent discharged from a sewage treatment plant were subjected to BOD test. The samples were labelled A, B and C; but the laboratory attendant did not note which was which. The BOD values of the three samples A, B and C were recorded as 20mg/L, 8mg/L and 400mg/L, respectively. Which sample of the water is most polluted? Can you assign the correct label to each assuming the river water is relatively clean?
solution: Sample C, with the highest BOD value of 400 mg/L, is the most polluted, since a higher BOD indicates a greater amount of organic matter present (requiring more oxygen for microbial breakdown), reflecting higher pollution. Based on relative pollution levels: Sample C (BOD = 400 mg/L) = untreated sewage water (highest organic load, most polluted); Sample A (BOD = 20 mg/L) = secondary effluent from the sewage treatment plant (organic load already substantially reduced by treatment, but still higher than clean river water); Sample B (BOD = 8 mg/L) = river water (relatively clean, lowest BOD).
steps: Higher BOD = more organic pollutant load = more polluted water
Sample C (400 mg/L) is the most polluted -> untreated sewage water
Sample A (20 mg/L), moderately polluted -> secondary (treated) effluent
Sample B (8 mg/L), least polluted -> relatively clean river water

question: Find out the name of the microbes from which Cyclosporin A (an immunosuppressive drug) and Statins (blood cholesterol lowering agents) are obtained.
solution: Cyclosporin A, an immunosuppressive drug used in organ-transplant patients to prevent graft rejection, is obtained from the fungus Trichoderma polysporum. Statins, used as blood cholesterol-lowering agents (they block the enzyme responsible for cholesterol synthesis), are produced by the yeast Monascus purpureus.
steps: Cyclosporin A (immunosuppressant) is produced by the fungus Trichoderma polysporum
Statins (cholesterol-lowering drugs) are produced by the yeast Monascus purpureus

question: Can you list 10 recombinant proteins which are used in medical practice? Find out where they are used as therapeutics (use the internet).
solution: Ten examples of recombinant therapeutic proteins used in medical practice: 1. Human insulin (Humulin) — used to treat diabetes mellitus. 2. Human growth hormone (Humatrope) — used to treat growth-hormone deficiency/dwarfism. 3. Erythropoietin — used to treat anaemia associated with chronic kidney disease. 4. Factor VIII — used to treat haemophilia A. 5. Hepatitis B surface antigen (recombinant vaccine) — used to vaccinate against hepatitis B. 6. Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) — used to dissolve blood clots in heart attack/stroke patients. 7. Interferon-alpha — used in treatment of certain cancers and viral infections (e.g., hepatitis C). 8. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) — used to stimulate white blood cell production, e.g., after chemotherapy. 9. DNase I (dornase alfa) — used in treatment of cystic fibrosis to reduce mucus viscosity. 10. Monoclonal antibodies (e.g., trastuzumab) — used to treat specific cancers such as breast cancer.
steps: Human insulin — diabetes treatment; Growth hormone — dwarfism/growth deficiency
Erythropoietin — anaemia in kidney disease; Factor VIII — haemophilia A
Hepatitis B surface antigen — vaccine; tPA — clot-dissolving in heart attack/stroke
Interferon-alpha, G-CSF, DNase I and monoclonal antibodies used in cancer, immune support and cystic fibrosis treatment respectively

question: Make a chart (with diagrammatic representation) showing a restriction enzyme, the substrate DNA on which it acts, the site at which it cuts DNA and the product it produces.
solution: Description of the chart (in words, since a diagram cannot be rendered here): Take the restriction enzyme EcoRI as an example. It acts on double-stranded DNA that contains its specific palindromic recognition sequence: 5'-GAATTC-3' / 3'-CTTAAG-5'. EcoRI cuts each strand between the G and A bases (i.e., between G and the following A) on both strands, at the same point within this palindromic sequence, producing two DNA fragments, each with single-stranded, complementary projecting ends called 'sticky ends' (5'-AATT overhang). These sticky ends can base-pair with any other DNA fragment cut with the same enzyme, which is exploited in recombinant DNA technology to join foreign DNA with vector DNA.
steps: Restriction enzyme example: EcoRI, recognition sequence 5'-GAATTC-3' (palindromic)
Substrate: double-stranded DNA containing this sequence
Cutting site: between G and A on each strand, symmetrically within the sequence
Product: two DNA fragments with complementary single-stranded 'sticky ends' (AATT overhang) that can re-anneal with other similarly cut DNA

question: From what you have learnt, can you tell whether enzymes are bigger or DNA is bigger in molecular size? How did you know?
solution: DNA is much bigger in molecular size compared to enzymes (proteins). This can be understood from the fact that a single gene itself, being a segment of DNA, is generally larger than the protein/enzyme it encodes, and the entire genomic DNA of an organism (consisting of millions to billions of base pairs, e.g., the human genome has about 3 x 10^9 base pairs) is vastly larger than any single enzyme molecule, which typically consists of only a few hundred amino acids. This can also be inferred practically — when DNA is cut with a restriction enzyme, even a very large number of small enzyme molecules are needed to act upon (and are much smaller than) the giant DNA molecule they cut.
steps: DNA (genome) consists of millions to billions of base pairs — an extremely long molecule
Enzymes/proteins are made of a few hundred amino acids at most — much smaller molecules
Even a single gene (part of DNA) is generally larger than the protein it encodes
Hence DNA is much bigger in molecular size than enzymes

question: What would be the molar concentration of human DNA in a human cell? Consult your teacher.
solution: The molar concentration of DNA in a human cell is extremely low, because although each human diploid cell contains a very long DNA molecule (about 6.6 x 10^9 base pairs, with an enormous molecular weight of the order of 10^12 daltons), there is essentially only one copy (one molecule, or 46 chromosomal DNA molecules) of this DNA present per cell, contained within the small volume of the nucleus. Using the formula for molarity (moles of DNA per litre of nuclear volume), since the number of DNA molecules per cell is extremely small (just a few, i.e. of the order of 10^-18 to 10^-20 moles) relative to Avogadro's number, and the nuclear volume is extremely small (of the order of picolitres), the molar concentration works out to be extremely low (of the order of nanomolar or less) — illustrating that although DNA has enormous molecular weight, its actual molar concentration in a cell is very small since only very few DNA molecules are present per cell.
steps: Human diploid cell has ~6.6x10^9 base pairs of DNA but essentially just 46 DNA molecules (chromosomes)
Molarity = moles of DNA / volume of nucleus; number of DNA molecules is extremely small in mole terms
Nuclear volume is also extremely small (picolitre range)
Net result: molar concentration of DNA in a cell is extremely low, despite DNA's enormous molecular weight

question: Do eukaryotic cells have restriction endonucleases? Justify your answer.
solution: No, restriction endonucleases (in the classical sense used in biotechnology) are not found in eukaryotic cells; they are found naturally only in prokaryotic cells (bacteria). Bacteria produce these enzymes as part of a restriction-modification system to protect themselves against invading foreign DNA (such as bacteriophage DNA) — the restriction enzyme cleaves and destroys any foreign DNA lacking the bacterium's own specific pattern of methylation, while the bacterium's own DNA is protected from digestion because it is appropriately methylated at the recognition sites by a companion modification (methylase) enzyme. Since eukaryotic cells do not need this particular bacterial defence mechanism against phage/foreign DNA in the same way, they do not naturally possess this class of restriction endonucleases.
steps: Restriction endonucleases are naturally found in bacteria (prokaryotes), not typically in eukaryotic cells
They form part of a bacterial restriction-modification defence system against invading (phage) DNA
Bacterium's own DNA is protected by methylation at the recognition sites (modification enzyme)
Eukaryotic cells lack this particular defence mechanism and hence do not naturally have such restriction enzymes

question: Besides better aeration and mixing properties, what other advantages do stirred tank bioreactors have over shake flasks?
solution: Besides better aeration and mixing, stirred-tank bioreactors offer several other advantages over small-scale shake flasks: they allow large-scale (industrial-volume) production of the desired product, unlike shake flasks which are limited to very small culture volumes; they have provision for maintaining and monitoring optimum growth conditions (such as temperature, pH, oxygen levels) throughout the process, allowing precise process control which is difficult in shake flasks; they typically have an agitator system to distribute the cells/nutrients and oxygen evenly throughout the vessel; an oxygen-delivery system to supply sufficient oxygen for the culture; a foam-control system to prevent excessive foam formation; and sampling ports that allow periodic withdrawal of small volumes of the culture for analysis/monitoring, all of which make consistent, controlled, large-scale (industrial) production of the biotechnological product possible.
steps: Bioreactors allow production at a much larger (industrial) scale than shake flasks
They provide precise control and monitoring of temperature, pH, oxygen and other growth conditions
Include agitator, oxygen-delivery and foam-control systems for consistent culture conditions
Have sampling ports for periodic monitoring, enabling reliable, scalable, industrial production

question: Collect 5 examples of palindromic DNA sequences by consulting your teacher. Better try to create a palindromic sequence by following base-pair rules.
solution:
Five examples of palindromic DNA sequences recognised by common restriction enzymes are:
1. EcoRI: 5'-GAATTC-3' / 3'-CTTAAG-5'
2. BamHI: 5'-GGATCC-3' / 3'-CCTAGG-5'
3. HindIII: 5'-AAGCTT-3' / 3'-TTCGAA-5'
4. PstI: 5'-CTGCAG-3' / 3'-GACGTC-5'
SalI: 5'-GTCGAC-3' / 3'-CAGCTG-5'
To construct a new palindromic sequence, choose a sequence for one strand and write its complementary strand in antiparallel (3'->5') orientation such that reading either strand in the 5'->3' direction gives the identical sequence, e.g., 5'-GGTACC-3' paired with 3'-CCATGG-5' — reading the bottom strand 5'->3' gives GGTACC, identical to the top strand, confirming it is palindromic.
steps: A DNA palindrome reads the same 5'->3' on both strands (complementary and symmetric)
Common examples: EcoRI (GAATTC), BamHI (GGATCC), HindIII (AAGCTT), PstI (CTGCAG), SalI (GTCGAC)
To construct one: pick a sequence, write its complementary antiparallel strand, and check both read identically 5'->3'
Example constructed: GGTACC / CCATGG is palindromic

question: Can you recall meiosis and indicate at what stage a recombinant DNA is made?
solution: During meiosis, natural genetic recombination occurs at the pachytene stage of prophase I (specifically during crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes), when a recombination nodule/complex is formed and genetic material is exchanged between the paired homologous chromosomes. This natural exchange of DNA segments between homologous chromosomes is analogous in principle to artificial recombinant DNA technology, where foreign DNA is deliberately combined with vector DNA in the laboratory using restriction enzymes and ligase.
steps: Natural recombination (crossing over) occurs during meiosis, specifically at the pachytene stage of prophase I
Involves exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
This natural process is the biological basis/inspiration behind the concept of 'recombinant' DNA
Artificial recombinant DNA technology instead uses restriction enzymes and ligase in vitro to combine foreign and vector DNA

question: Can you think and answer how a reporter enzyme can be used to monitor transformation of host cells by foreign DNA in addition to a selectable marker?
solution: A reporter gene codes for a reporter enzyme/protein whose activity can be easily detected and measured, and it can be inserted into the vector such that it is inactivated (insertional inactivation) when a foreign DNA fragment is inserted at a particular site within it. Cells that have taken up recombinant DNA (with the foreign gene inserted inside the reporter gene) will fail to produce a functional reporter enzyme, whereas cells with non-recombinant vector DNA (no foreign gene inserted) will still express the functional reporter enzyme. For example, using the enzyme beta-galactosidase as a reporter: if the foreign DNA is inserted within the beta-galactosidase gene sequence, recombinant colonies do not produce the enzyme and therefore, on a medium containing a chromogenic substrate, remain colourless, while non-recombinant colonies (with an intact, functional beta-galactosidase gene) turn blue. This allows recombinants to be easily distinguished from non-recombinants visually, without needing to test for antibiotic resistance/selectable markers alone.
steps: Reporter gene (e.g., beta-galactosidase) is placed at the site of foreign-DNA insertion in the vector
Successful insertion of foreign DNA disrupts (inactivates) the reporter gene — insertional inactivation
Recombinant colonies fail to express the reporter enzyme; non-recombinant colonies still express it
Using a chromogenic substrate, recombinants appear colourless while non-recombinants turn blue, allowing visual screening alongside selectable markers

question:
Describe briefly the following:
(a) Origin of replication
(b) Bioreactors
(c) Downstream processing
solution:
(a) Origin of replication (ori): A specific sequence on a vector/plasmid DNA from where replication of the DNA molecule starts; a piece of DNA linked to this sequence can be replicated within the host cell, and this sequence is also responsible for controlling the copy number of the linked DNA — vectors with an ori that gives a high copy number are preferred for cloning to obtain multiple copies of the target DNA.
(b) Bioreactors: Large vessels (of volumes ranging from litres to thousands of litres) in which raw materials are biologically converted, using microbes/plant/animal cells or enzymes, into specific products, individual enzymes, etc., under optimum growth conditions (temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen) with continuous monitoring, allowing large-scale (industrial) production. A commonly used bioreactor is the stirred-tank type.
(c) Downstream processing: The series of processes carried out after the biosynthetic (fermentation) stage of a bioprocess, in which the product is separated/purified and formulated with suitable preservatives, including steps such as separation and purification of the product, and stringent quality-control testing for each product, before it is marketed as a finished commercial product; the process employed will vary depending on the nature of the product.
steps: Origin of replication (ori): sequence in vector DNA where replication starts and which controls copy number
Bioreactors: large vessels for biological conversion of raw materials into products under controlled optimum conditions at industrial scale
Downstream processing: post-fermentation steps of separation, purification, quality-control testing and formulation of the final product

question:
Explain briefly
(a) PCR
(b) Restriction enzymes and DNA
(c) Chitinase
solution:
(a) PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction): An in vitro technique used to amplify (make multiple copies of) a specific segment/gene of DNA using two sets of short, chemically synthesised oligonucleotide primers complementary to the two ends of the target DNA region, a heat-stable DNA polymerase enzyme (e.g., Taq polymerase, isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus), and repeated cycles of denaturation (heating to separate DNA strands), annealing (cooling to allow primers to bind) and extension (polymerase synthesises new complementary strands), resulting in exponential amplification of the target DNA sequence.
(b) Restriction enzymes and DNA: Restriction enzymes are a class of enzymes (belonging to a larger class called nucleases) that cut DNA at specific sequences known as recognition sequences, which are typically palindromic. There are two categories: exonucleases, which remove nucleotides from the ends of the DNA, and endonucleases, which make cuts at specific positions within the DNA. Restriction endonucleases recognise and bind to a specific palindromic DNA sequence and cut both strands of the DNA at specific points within this sequence, producing fragments with either sticky or blunt ends, which is exploited to cut and join (recombine) DNA molecules in genetic engineering.
(c) Chitinase: An enzyme that degrades chitin, the major component of the fungal cell wall; it is used in biotechnology to break down and remove the fungal cell wall (along with cellulase, which digests plant cell walls) to obtain the 'naked' protoplast for use in techniques such as protoplast fusion in genetic engineering.
steps: PCR uses primers, Taq polymerase, and repeated denaturation-annealing-extension cycles to amplify a target DNA sequence exponentially
Restriction enzymes (endonucleases) cut DNA at specific palindromic recognition sequences, producing sticky/blunt ends used to cut and join DNA
Chitinase degrades fungal cell wall chitin, used (with cellulase) to obtain protoplasts for genetic engineering techniques

question:
Discuss with your teacher and find out how to distinguish between
(a) Plasmid DNA and Chromosomal DNA
(b) RNA and DNA
(c) Exonuclease and Endonuclease
solution:
(a) Plasmid DNA and Chromosomal DNA: Chromosomal DNA is the main, large genomic DNA of a bacterial cell that carries essential genes for normal survival and growth, present as a single circular molecule. Plasmid DNA is a small, extra-chromosomal, autonomously self-replicating (having its own origin of replication), usually circular DNA molecule that carries non-essential (but often useful, e.g., antibiotic resistance) genes, and can be separated from chromosomal DNA in the laboratory by techniques exploiting their difference in size and supercoiled nature (e.g., using density-based centrifugation, since plasmid DNA does not denature as easily as the larger chromosomal DNA when treated with alkali/heat).
(b) RNA and DNA: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) contains the sugar deoxyribose, the base thymine (instead of uracil), and is typically double-stranded; it is the stable, long-term store of genetic information. RNA (ribonucleic acid) contains the sugar ribose, the base uracil (instead of thymine), and is typically single-stranded; it functions mainly in gene expression (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) or, in some viruses, as the genetic material itself. DNA and RNA can be distinguished experimentally, e.g., DNA is more chemically stable and resistant to alkaline hydrolysis, whereas RNA is readily hydrolysed by alkali due to the reactive 2'-OH group of ribose.
(c) Exonuclease and Endonuclease: Exonucleases remove nucleotides progressively from the free ends (5' or 3') of a DNA/RNA molecule. Endonucleases make cuts at specific internal positions within the DNA/RNA molecule, not from the ends. Restriction endonucleases are a special type of endonuclease that recognise and cut DNA only at specific palindromic recognition sequences.
steps: Chromosomal DNA is the main essential genomic DNA; plasmid DNA is small, extra-chromosomal, self-replicating and separable by size/density-based methods
DNA has deoxyribose sugar, thymine base, usually double-stranded and chemically more stable; RNA has ribose sugar, uracil base, usually single-stranded and less stable (alkali-sensitive)
Exonucleases cut nucleotides from the free ends of DNA/RNA; endonucleases cut at internal specific positions (restriction endonucleases are sequence-specific endonucleases)

question: Which part of the plant is best suited for making virus-free plants and why?
solution: The meristematic tissue (apical/shoot meristem tip) of the plant is best suited for producing virus-free plants. This is because even in a plant that is systemically infected with a virus, the meristematic region (the actively dividing tip of the shoot) is generally free of the virus, since the virus particles move/spread through the plant more slowly (via the vascular tissue) than the rate at which the meristem cells actively divide and grow, so the growing tip effectively 'outgrows' the infection. By excising this meristem tip and growing it using tissue culture (meristem culture) techniques, new plants that are free of the virus can be regenerated.
steps: Meristematic tissue (shoot apical meristem) is best suited for virus-free plant production
Viruses spread more slowly through the plant than the meristem cells' growth rate
The actively growing meristem tip usually remains free of virus even in an infected plant
Culturing the excised meristem tip (meristem culture) regenerates virus-free plants

question: What is the major advantage of producing plants by micropropagation?
solution: The major advantage of micropropagation is that it allows production of a very large number of genetically identical plants (clones) from a single parent plant, in a short time and in a limited space, using tissue culture techniques. This ensures that the desirable characteristics (like disease resistance, high yield, quality) of the selected parent plant are precisely retained in all the progeny plants, unlike sexual reproduction, which can introduce variation. It is especially useful for rapid, large-scale multiplication of ornamental plants, and of plants that are otherwise difficult to propagate (e.g., produce very few or no viable seeds).
steps: Micropropagation produces a large number of genetically identical (clonal) plants rapidly
Requires only a small amount of starting plant tissue and limited space/time
Ensures desirable parental traits are precisely retained (no genetic variation, unlike seed propagation)
Especially useful for plants difficult to propagate by seeds, and for rapid multiplication of elite/ornamental varieties

question: Find out what the various components of the medium used for propagation of an explant in vitro are?
solution: The nutrient medium used for in vitro propagation of an explant (tissue culture medium) typically consists of: (i) inorganic (macro- and micro-) nutrients/mineral salts required for plant growth, such as nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulphur and trace elements like iron, zinc, manganese, boron, copper; (ii) organic nutrients, mainly a carbon source such as sucrose (or another sugar), providing energy since the explant usually cannot photosynthesise adequately in culture; (iii) vitamins (such as thiamine, nicotinic acid, pyridoxine) and amino acids; (iv) plant growth regulators/hormones, such as auxins and cytokinins, in specific proportions to induce cell division, shoot and root formation as required; and (v) a gelling/solidifying agent, usually agar, if a solid (rather than liquid) medium is required.
steps: Inorganic mineral nutrients (macro- and micronutrients) needed for growth
Organic carbon source (usually sucrose) providing energy since explant cannot photosynthesise adequately
Vitamins and amino acids as growth supplements
Plant growth regulators (auxins, cytokinins) to control differentiation, plus agar as a solidifying agent for solid media

question:
Crystals of Bt toxin produced by some bacteria do not kill the bacteria themselves because –
(a) bacteria are resistant to the toxin
(b) toxin is immature
(c) toxin is inactive
(d) bacteria encloses toxin in a special sac.
solution: The correct answer is (c) toxin is inactive. Bt toxin is produced by Bacillus thuringiensis as inactive protoxin crystals. The protoxin does not harm the bacterium itself because it remains in an inactive form within the bacterium. It becomes active (toxic) only after it is ingested by a susceptible insect and is converted to its active form by the alkaline pH of the insect's gut, where it then binds to the gut epithelium and causes the death of the insect larva.
steps: Bt produces the toxin in an inactive (protoxin) crystalline form within the bacterium
It remains harmless to the bacterium itself in this inactive state
Activation occurs only in the alkaline gut environment of a susceptible insect after ingestion
Correct option: (c) toxin is inactive

question: What are transgenic bacteria? Illustrate using any one example.
solution: Transgenic bacteria are bacteria into whose genome a foreign gene (from another organism) has been artificially introduced using recombinant DNA technology, so that they express the product coded by that foreign gene. Example: transgenic Escherichia coli bacteria have been engineered to produce human insulin. The gene sequences coding for the A and B chains of human insulin were separately inserted into plasmid vectors and introduced into E. coli, which then produce the A and B polypeptide chains of insulin separately; these are then extracted and combined by forming disulphide bonds to form active human insulin, marketed as Humulin — this was the first genetically engineered/transgenic-bacteria-derived product approved for human use.
steps: Transgenic bacteria carry a foreign gene inserted via recombinant DNA technology
Example: E. coli engineered with human insulin A- and B-chain genes
The bacteria express the A and B polypeptide chains separately, which are extracted and joined by disulphide bonds
This produced Humulin, the first recombinant-bacteria-derived human insulin

question: Compare and contrast the advantages and disadvantages of production of genetically modified crops.
solution:
Advantages of GM crops: they can be made more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt); reduce dependence on chemical pesticides (e.g., Bt cotton, resistant to bollworm attack); reduce post-harvest losses; increase efficiency of mineral usage by plants (preventing early exhaustion of soil fertility); enhance nutritional value of food (e.g., Golden Rice, enriched with vitamin A); and can help meet increased food demand through higher yields and pest/disease resistance.
Disadvantages/concerns: possible unintended and unpredictable effects on the ecosystem, e.g., harmful effects on non-target/beneficial organisms; concerns over the potential of transgenes escaping into wild relatives through cross-pollination, creating 'superweeds'; possible allergenic or toxic effects of the new gene product on humans/animals consuming the GM food; increased dependence of farmers on seed companies for genetically modified seeds (which cannot always be saved and reused); high cost of developing GM crops; and ethical/socio-economic concerns and lack of long-term data on health/environmental safety.
steps: Advantages: pest/stress resistance, reduced pesticide use, better nutrition (e.g. Golden Rice), higher yields, reduced post-harvest losses
Disadvantages: possible ecological risks to non-target organisms, gene flow to wild relatives, potential allergenicity/toxicity
Also: farmer dependence on seed companies, high development cost, ethical and long-term safety concerns

question: What are Cry proteins? Name an organism that produce it. How has man exploited this protein to his benefit?
solution: Cry proteins (crystal proteins) are insecticidal proteins produced by the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), encoded by a group of genes called cry genes. Different Bt strains produce different Cry proteins that are specifically toxic to different groups of insects — for example, Cry I Ac and Cry II Ab control the cotton bollworm, Cry I Ab controls corn borer. Man has exploited these proteins by isolating the specific cry genes from Bacillus thuringiensis and introducing them into crop plants through genetic engineering (e.g., Bt cotton, Bt brinjal), so that the plant itself produces the toxin and becomes resistant to attack by specific insect pests without requiring the application of chemical pesticides, since the toxin, once ingested by the insect, gets activated in its alkaline gut and kills the pest, but is harmless to humans and other non-target organisms.
steps: Cry proteins are insecticidal crystal proteins produced by Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt)
Different Cry proteins (e.g., Cry I Ac, Cry II Ab) are toxic to specific insect groups
Man isolated cry genes and introduced them into crop plants (e.g., Bt cotton) via genetic engineering
This makes the crop resistant to specific pests, reducing chemical pesticide use, since the toxin is activated only in the insect's alkaline gut

question: What is gene therapy? Illustrate using the example of adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.
solution: Gene therapy is a method to correct a genetic defect diagnosed in a child/embryo by inserting a normal, functional gene into the individual's cells (or germ line) to replace/compensate for the defective mutant allele responsible for the disorder. Illustration using ADA deficiency: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency is caused by the deletion or a mutation in the gene coding for the enzyme ADA, an enzyme crucial for normal immune function; its deficiency causes a form of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). Traditionally it could be treated by bone-marrow transplantation (not fully curative) or enzyme replacement therapy (through periodic injections of functional ADA, an expensive and non-permanent solution). Gene therapy provides a permanent cure: lymphocytes from the patient's blood are grown in culture outside the body, and a normal, functional copy of the ADA gene is introduced into these lymphocytes using a retroviral vector, which are then reintroduced into the patient's body. However, since these lymphocytes are not immortal, the patient requires periodic infusion of such genetically engineered lymphocytes. A more permanent cure would be achieved if the ADA gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages, so that the corrected gene is present in all the cells produced from these cells throughout the individual's life.
steps: Gene therapy inserts a normal, functional gene to correct/compensate for a genetically defective gene
ADA deficiency is caused by deletion/mutation of the gene for ADA enzyme, leading to SCID
In gene therapy, patient's lymphocytes are cultured, given a functional ADA gene via a retroviral vector, and reinfused
Since lymphocytes are not immortal, periodic treatment is needed; a permanent cure requires correcting the gene in early embryonic/stem cells

question: Diagrammatically represent the experimental steps in cloning and expressing an human gene (say the gene for growth hormone) into a bacterium like E. coli?
solution: Description of the experimental steps (since a diagram cannot be rendered here): (1) Isolation of the desired human gene (e.g., the gene coding for growth hormone) from human DNA, or synthesis of its cDNA from the corresponding mRNA using reverse transcriptase. (2) Selection of a suitable cloning vector (a bacterial plasmid) containing an origin of replication, a selectable marker gene, and a unique restriction site. (3) Cutting both the isolated human gene and the plasmid vector with the same restriction enzyme, producing complementary sticky ends. (4) Ligating (joining) the human gene into the cut plasmid using the enzyme DNA ligase, forming a recombinant DNA (rDNA) molecule. (5) Introducing this recombinant plasmid into a competent host bacterium such as E. coli, through a process called transformation. (6) Selecting the transformed bacteria that have taken up the recombinant plasmid, using the selectable marker (e.g., antibiotic resistance gene) present on the vector. (7) Allowing the transformed E. coli to multiply in a bioreactor under optimum conditions, during which the inserted human gene is transcribed and translated by the bacterial machinery, so that the bacteria express and secrete the human growth hormone protein. (8) Finally, downstream processing — extraction, purification and formulation of the growth hormone protein for use.
steps: Isolate the human gene (or make cDNA from its mRNA using reverse transcriptase)
Cut both the gene and a plasmid vector with the same restriction enzyme, then ligate them with DNA ligase to form recombinant DNA
Transform the recombinant plasmid into E. coli and select transformants using a marker gene
Grow transformed E. coli in a bioreactor; the bacteria express and secrete the human growth hormone, which is then purified by downstream processing

question: Can you suggest a method to remove oil (hydrocarbon) from seeds based on your understanding of rDNA technology and chemistry of oil?
solution: Based on the understanding that oils/hydrocarbons are naturally broken down (degraded) by certain microorganisms, a genetically engineered approach could involve identifying and isolating genes from microbes capable of producing oil/hydrocarbon-degrading enzymes (lipases and related enzymes, similar in principle to those in oil-degrading, 'superbug' type bacteria used in bioremediation of oil spills), and using rDNA technology to introduce and express these enzyme-coding genes appropriately (e.g., within the seed tissue itself or in a microbial system used for seed/oil processing) to enzymatically break down the oil/hydrocarbon content within the seed into simpler, easily extractable or non-oily by-products, thereby helping remove oil from the seed material through a biological/enzymatic (rather than only mechanical/solvent-based) process.
steps: Oils are hydrocarbons that can be broken down by specific microbial enzymes (e.g., lipases)
Using rDNA technology, genes for such oil-degrading enzymes could be identified and introduced into a suitable host/system
The expressed enzymes can hydrolyse/degrade the oil within the seed into simpler, extractable products
This offers a biotechnological, enzyme-based alternative/supplement to conventional mechanical or solvent extraction of oil from seeds

question: Find out from internet what is golden rice.
solution: Golden Rice is a genetically modified variety of rice that has been engineered to biosynthesise beta-carotene (a precursor of vitamin A) in the edible part of the rice grain (endosperm), giving the grain a golden-yellow colour. It was developed by introducing genes involved in the beta-carotene biosynthetic pathway (originally from daffodil and later improved using genes from maize, along with a gene from a soil bacterium) into the rice genome. It was developed to address vitamin A deficiency, a major public health problem causing blindness and other health issues in populations that rely heavily on rice as a staple food and have limited access to vitamin-A-rich foods.
steps: Golden Rice is a transgenic rice variety engineered to produce beta-carotene (provitamin A) in its edible grain
This gives the grain a characteristic golden-yellow colour
Developed by introducing beta-carotene biosynthesis pathway genes (e.g. from daffodil/maize and a bacterium) into rice
Aim: address vitamin A deficiency in populations dependent on rice as a staple food

question: Does our blood have proteases and nucleases?
solution: Yes, human blood does contain proteases and nucleases. Blood plasma contains various proteolytic enzymes (proteases) involved in processes such as blood clotting (e.g., thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin) and the complement system of immunity. Nucleases (enzymes that degrade nucleic acids) are also present in blood/serum, which break down any free-circulating DNA/RNA (e.g., released from dying cells or foreign sources), helping to protect the body. This presence of nucleases and proteases in blood is an important practical consideration in biotechnology — it is one of the reasons therapeutic proteins/DNA (e.g., insulin, or DNA-based vaccines/drugs) usually cannot simply be taken orally, since they would be degraded by such enzymes present in blood and the digestive system before reaching their target.
steps: Yes, blood contains proteases (e.g., thrombin, complement proteins) involved in clotting and immunity
Blood also contains nucleases that degrade free circulating nucleic acids
This is relevant to biotechnology, since it explains why protein/DNA-based drugs are often degraded if taken orally and need special delivery methods
Hence therapeutic proteins are generally administered by injection rather than orally

question: Consult internet and find out how to make orally active protein pharmaceutical. What is the major problem to be encountered?
solution: To make a protein pharmaceutical orally active, approaches include: encapsulating the protein drug in protective carriers (such as liposomes, nanoparticles, or specialised polymer coatings) that shield it from degradation by digestive enzymes (proteases) and the highly acidic environment of the stomach until it reaches the site of absorption; chemically modifying the protein (e.g., PEGylation) to increase its stability and resistance to enzymatic breakdown; or co-administering enzyme inhibitors/absorption enhancers along with the protein. The major problem encountered is that proteins, being made of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, are readily degraded/digested by the proteolytic enzymes (proteases) and the acidic pH present in the stomach and intestine when taken orally, just like any other dietary protein, drastically reducing their bioavailability and therapeutic effectiveness — hence most protein-based drugs (like insulin) must currently be administered by injection rather than orally.
steps: Approaches: protective encapsulation (liposomes/nanoparticles), chemical modification (e.g., PEGylation), or co-administered protective agents
Major problem: proteins are degraded by proteases and stomach acid when taken orally, just like dietary protein
This drastically reduces bioavailability of protein drugs given orally
Hence most protein therapeutics (e.g., insulin) are currently given by injection, not orally

question: List the attributes that populations possess but not individuals.
solution: Populations possess certain group-level attributes that an individual organism does not have. These include: birth rate (natality) and death rate (mortality) — an individual is simply born or dies, but a population has a rate of births/deaths; sex ratio — an individual is either male or female, but a population has a definable ratio of males to females; age distribution/age structure — the proportion of individuals of different ages, often represented as an age pyramid; and population density — the number of individuals per unit area/volume, which is meaningful only for a population, not a single organism.
steps: Birth rate (natality) and death rate (mortality) are population-level attributes
Sex ratio is meaningful for a population (an individual is simply male or female)
Age distribution/age structure describes proportion of individuals of different ages in a population
Population density (number per unit area) applies only to populations, not individuals

question: If a population growing exponentially double in size in 3 years, what is the intrinsic rate of increase (r) of the population?
solution: For exponential growth, Nt = N0 * e^(rt). If the population doubles, Nt = 2N0, so 2N0 = N0 * e^(r*3), giving 2 = e^(3r). Taking natural log on both sides: ln 2 = 3r, so r = ln 2 / 3 = 0.693/3 ≈ 0.231 per year (approximately 0.23 year^-1).
steps: Exponential growth equation: Nt = N0 e^(rt)
Doubling means Nt = 2N0, giving 2 = e^(rt) with t = 3 years
Taking natural log: ln2 = 3r

question: Name important defence mechanisms in plants against herbivory.
solution: Plants have evolved several defence mechanisms against herbivory (being eaten by herbivores): morphological defences, such as thorns (e.g., in Acacia, Cactus), which serve as a mechanical deterrent to grazing/browsing animals; and chemical defences, in which plants produce and store a variety of chemical substances that make the plant tissue unpalatable, toxic, or harmful to herbivores when eaten — examples include nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine, opium, etc. produced by various plants, some of which can even kill or severely sicken the herbivore, or at least discourage it from feeding on the plant again.
steps: Morphological defence: thorns/spines (e.g., in Acacia, Cactus) deter grazing/browsing
Chemical defence: production of toxic/bitter/unpalatable secondary metabolites in plant tissues
Examples of such defence chemicals: nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine, opium
These chemicals make the plant unpalatable or toxic, discouraging herbivory

question: An orchid plant is growing on the branch of mango tree. How do you describe this interaction between the orchid and the mango tree?
solution: This interaction is an example of commensalism, in which the orchid (epiphyte) benefits by using the branch of the mango tree simply as a surface/support for growing (gaining better access to sunlight, air and moisture), without deriving any nutrition from the mango tree and without harming it in any way, while the mango tree itself is neither benefited nor harmed by the presence of the orchid.
steps: The orchid is an epiphyte growing on the mango tree purely for physical support
It does not draw nutrients from the mango tree (unlike a parasite) and does not harm it
The mango tree is unaffected — neither benefited nor harmed
This one-sided-benefit, no-harm relationship defines commensalism

question: What is the ecological principle behind the biological control method of managing with pest insects?
solution: The ecological principle behind biological pest control is the predator-prey (or parasite/pathogen-host) relationship, in which a natural enemy (predator, parasite or pathogen) of the pest species is deliberately introduced or encouraged to keep the population of the pest insect under check, since predators are known to play a key role in regulating and reducing the prey (pest) population to a low, manageable level without eliminating the pest population entirely (which would also destroy the natural enemy's own resource/food base), thus achieving a stable, balanced control of the pest population without the need for chemical pesticides. A classic example is the control of the cottony cushion scale insect pest of citrus trees using its natural predator, a beetle (Rodolia/Vedalia beetle).
steps: Principle: predator-prey (or host-parasite) relationship used to naturally regulate pest population
A natural enemy of the pest is introduced/encouraged, which reduces (but does not eliminate) the pest population
This keeps the pest at a manageable, low density without chemical pesticides
Classic example: Vedalia beetle used to control the cottony cushion scale insect on citrus

question: Define population and community.
solution:
Population: A group of individuals of the same species living together in a particular geographical area at a given time, which are actually or potentially interbreeding among themselves.
Community: An assemblage of populations of different species (of plants, animals and microbes) that live together, interact with one another, and share the same habitat in a given geographical area.
steps: Population = group of individuals of one species in a given area, capable of interbreeding
Community = assemblage of populations of different species living and interacting together in an area

question:
Define the following terms and give one example for each:
(a) Commensalism
(b) Parasitism
(c) Camouflage
(d) Mutualism
(e) Interspecific competition
solution:
(a) Commensalism: An interaction between two species in which one species benefits while the other is neither harmed nor benefited. Example: an orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch.
(b) Parasitism: An interaction in which one organism (the parasite) derives nutrition and benefit at the expense of, and to the detriment of, another organism (the host), often living on or inside the host's body. Example: Plasmodium (the malarial parasite) living in a human host, or a tapeworm living in the intestine of humans.
(c) Camouflage: A defence adaptation in which an organism's body colouration/pattern blends with its surroundings, making it difficult for a predator (or prey) to detect it. Example: the pale-green colouration and leaf-like shape of the stick insect and many insects that blend with the vegetation they live on, escaping predation.
(d) Mutualism: An interaction between two species in which both species benefit from each other. Example: the mutualistic relationship between lichens (algae and fungi living together) or the pollination mutualism between the fig plant and its specific pollinating wasp species.
(e) Interspecific competition: Competition for the same limited resource(s) (food, space, etc.) between individuals belonging to two (or more) different species. Example: competition between resident barbet and mynah birds for nest holes in trees, or between flamingoes and resident fish in some lakes for the same zooplankton food.
steps: Commensalism: one benefits, other unaffected — e.g., orchid on mango tree
Parasitism: one benefits at the cost/harm of the other (host) — e.g., Plasmodium in humans
Camouflage: colour/pattern blending with surroundings to avoid detection — e.g., stick insect
Mutualism: both species benefit — e.g., lichens (fungus+alga), fig-wasp pollination
Interspecific competition: two different species compete for the same resource — e.g., barbet vs mynah for nesting holes

question: With the help of suitable diagram describe the logistic population growth curve.
solution: The logistic growth model describes population growth in an environment with limited resources, where growth rate decreases as population size approaches the carrying capacity (K) of the habitat, following the equation dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K, where N is population size, r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase, and K is the carrying capacity. When plotted (population size N on the y-axis against time on the x-axis), the resulting curve is S-shaped (sigmoid), consisting of an initial phase of slow growth (lag phase, when population is small), followed by a phase of rapid, near-exponential growth as resources are still abundant, and finally a phase where growth rate slows down and the curve flattens out (plateaus) as the population size approaches the carrying capacity K of the habitat, beyond which the population size stabilises since resources become limiting. This is considered a more realistic model of population growth than the exponential (J-shaped) model, since resources for growth (food, space) are finite in nature and cannot support unlimited/exponential growth indefinitely.
steps: Logistic growth equation: dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K, incorporating carrying capacity K
The growth curve is S-shaped (sigmoid) when N is plotted against time
Phases: initial slow (lag) growth, rapid near-exponential growth, then slowing and levelling off near K
Population stabilises at carrying capacity K, since resources are limited — more realistic than unchecked exponential growth

question:
Select the statement which explains best parasitism.
(a) One organism is benefited.
(b) Both the organisms are benefited.
(c) One organism is benefited, other is not affected.
(d) One organism is benefited, other is affected.
solution: The correct answer is (d) One organism is benefited, other is affected. In parasitism, the parasite benefits (gains nutrition/resources) at the direct expense and detriment (harm) of the host organism, distinguishing it from commensalism (option c, where the other organism is unaffected) and mutualism (option b, where both benefit).
steps: Parasitism involves one organism (parasite) gaining benefit while harming the other (host)
This distinguishes it from commensalism (other unaffected) and mutualism (both benefit)
Correct option: (d) one organism is benefited, other is affected (harmed)

question: List any three important characteristics of a population and explain.
solution:
Three important characteristics of a population are:
1. Population density: The size of a population relative to a given unit of space/area at a given time, usually the most appropriate measure of population size, expressed as the number of individuals per unit area or volume.
2. Natality and mortality (birth and death rates): Natality refers to the number of births in the population during a given time period relative to population size (increases population size), while mortality refers to the number of deaths in the population in that period (decreases population size); together they determine the growth rate of the population.
3. Age distribution (age structure/age pyramid): The proportion of individuals of various ages in a population relative to the total population, which can be graphically represented as an age pyramid; the shape of this pyramid (expanding, stable or declining) reflects whether the population is growing, stationary or declining.
steps: Population density: number of individuals per unit area/volume, the primary measure of population size
Natality (birth rate) and mortality (death rate) together determine net population growth rate
Age distribution/age pyramid: proportion of individuals of different ages, indicating whether population is growing, stable or declining

question:
Fill in the blanks.
(a) Plants are called as_________because they fix carbon dioxide.
(b) In an ecosystem dominated by trees, the pyramid (of numbers) is_________type.
(c) In aquatic ecosystems, the limiting factor for the productivity is_________.
(d) Common detritivores in our ecosystem are_________.
(e) The major reservoir of carbon on earth is_________.
solution:
(a) Producers (autotrophs) — because they fix atmospheric carbon dioxide through photosynthesis.
(b) Inverted (spindle-shaped) — since a few large trees (producers) support progressively larger numbers of smaller herbivores and carnivores at higher trophic levels.
(c) Light (sunlight penetration) — in deeper water bodies, availability of light is usually the limiting factor for productivity.
(d) Earthworms, and various soil organisms/insects such as beetles, ants, millipedes and fungi/bacteria that act as detritivores/decomposers.
(e) Oceans (the ocean/marine reservoir, mainly as dissolved carbon dioxide and carbonates) — the largest reservoir of carbon on Earth.
steps: (a) Producers fix CO2 via photosynthesis
(b) Tree-dominated ecosystem gives an inverted/spindle-shaped pyramid of numbers
(c) Light availability is usually the limiting factor for aquatic productivity
(d) Earthworms and similar soil organisms are common detritivores
(e) Oceans form the largest reservoir of carbon on Earth

question:
Which one of the following has the largest population in a food chain?
(a) Producers
(b) Primary consumers
(c) Secondary consumers
(d) Decomposers
solution: The correct answer is (a) Producers. Producers occupy the first (base) trophic level of a food chain and have the largest population/biomass, since energy and biomass decrease progressively at each successive trophic level (primary consumers, secondary consumers, and so on) due to loss of energy at each transfer, following the pyramid of numbers/biomass, which is typically upright (broad base, narrowing towards the top) in most terrestrial ecosystems.
steps: Producers form the base of the food chain and have the largest numbers/biomass
Population/energy decreases at each successive trophic level (10% law)
This gives an upright pyramid of numbers/biomass in most ecosystems
Correct option: (a) Producers

question:
The second trophic level in a lake is
(a) Phytoplankton
(b) Zooplankton
(c) Benthos
(d) Fishes
solution: The correct answer is (b) Zooplankton. In a lake ecosystem, phytoplankton (algae) are the producers occupying the first trophic level; zooplankton, which feed directly on phytoplankton, are the primary consumers occupying the second trophic level.
steps: First trophic level in a lake = phytoplankton (producers)
Second trophic level = primary consumers that feed on phytoplankton
Zooplankton feed directly on phytoplankton
Correct option: (b) Zooplankton

question:
Secondary producers are
(a) Herbivores
(b) Producers
(c) Carnivores
(d) None of the above
solution: The correct answer is (d) None of the above. The term 'secondary producers' is not a standard ecological category — only green plants/autotrophs are producers (primary producers), since they alone can fix carbon/produce organic matter from inorganic sources using light energy. Herbivores are primary consumers and carnivores are secondary/tertiary consumers, not producers.
steps: Only autotrophs (green plants, some bacteria/algae) qualify as producers
There is no standard category called 'secondary producers' in ecology
Herbivores are primary consumers; carnivores are secondary/tertiary consumers
Correct option: (d) None of the above

question:
What is the percentage of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) in the incident solar radiation?
(a) 100%
(b) 50 %
(c) 1-5%
(d) 2-10%
solution: The correct answer is (b) 50%. Of the total incident solar radiation, only about 50% is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), i.e., radiation of wavelengths that can be used by plants for photosynthesis; however, plants ultimately fix only about 2-10% of this PAR into chemical energy (gross primary productivity) due to various losses.
steps: Total incident solar radiation includes wavelengths usable and not usable for photosynthesis
About 50% of incident solar radiation qualifies as photosynthetically active radiation (PAR)
Correct option: (b) 50%
(Note: plants fix only about 2-10% of PAR as chemical energy — a separate figure from the PAR percentage itself)

question:
Distinguish between
(a) Grazing food chain and detritus food chain
(b) Production and decomposition
(c) Upright and inverted pyramid
(d) Food chain and Food web
(e) Litter and detritus
(f) Primary and secondary productivity
solution:
(a) Grazing food chain and detritus food chain: The grazing food chain (GFC) begins with living green plants (producers) as the base, energy flowing from producers to herbivores and then to carnivores. The detritus food chain (DFC) begins with dead organic matter (detritus), which is broken down by decomposers/detritivores, and this chain generally dominates in terms of energy flow in most ecosystems.
(b) Production and decomposition: Production is the process by which producers (via photosynthesis) or consumers accumulate biomass/energy (organic matter) in an ecosystem. Decomposition is the breakdown of complex dead organic matter (detritus) into inorganic substances by decomposers, releasing nutrients back into the ecosystem for reuse.
(c) Upright and inverted pyramid: An upright pyramid has a large base of producers, narrowing progressively at successive trophic levels (typical for pyramid of numbers/biomass in most terrestrial ecosystems). An inverted pyramid has a narrow base of producers and expands at higher trophic levels (e.g., pyramid of numbers in a tree ecosystem, or pyramid of biomass in some aquatic/pond ecosystems where phytoplankton biomass is low but supports larger consumer biomass).
(d) Food chain and Food web: A food chain is a single, linear sequence of organisms through which energy/food flows, each organism feeding on the one before it. A food web is a network of several interconnected food chains existing together in an ecosystem, representing the various alternative pathways of energy flow.
(e) Litter and detritus: Litter refers to the fresh, undecomposed or partially decomposed dead plant remains (leaves, twigs, bark, etc.) that fall on the ground, forming the raw material for detritus. Detritus refers to the broader category of all dead organic matter, including plant litter as well as animal remains/faecal matter, which forms the base of the detritus food chain and is acted upon by decomposers.
(f) Primary and secondary productivity: Primary productivity is the rate of production/biomass generation by producers (autotrophs) through photosynthesis, expressed as gross primary productivity (GPP, total fixation) and net primary productivity (NPP = GPP minus respiratory losses). Secondary productivity is the rate of formation of new organic matter/biomass by consumers (herbivores/carnivores) through assimilation of the food they consume.
steps: Grazing food chain starts with living plants; detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter
Production = biomass/energy accumulation; decomposition = breakdown of dead matter releasing nutrients
Upright pyramid narrows at higher levels; inverted pyramid widens at higher levels
Food chain = single linear energy-flow sequence; food web = interconnected network of food chains
Litter = fresh dead plant material; detritus = all dead organic matter (plant + animal)
Primary productivity = rate of biomass production by producers; secondary productivity = rate of biomass formation by consumers

question: Describe the components of an ecosystem.
solution: An ecosystem consists of two main components: (1) Abiotic components — the non-living physical and chemical factors of the environment, including climatic factors (temperature, light, rainfall, humidity) and edaphic (soil-related) factors, as well as inorganic substances (like carbon, nitrogen, water, minerals) and organic compounds (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids) which link the biotic and abiotic components through the cycling of materials. (2) Biotic components — the living organisms present in the ecosystem, further classified as: Producers (autotrophs), mainly green plants and some bacteria/algae, which fix inorganic carbon dioxide via photosynthesis to produce organic matter, forming the base of the food chain; Consumers (heterotrophs), which depend directly or indirectly on producers for food, classified as primary consumers/herbivores (feed directly on producers), secondary consumers/carnivores (feed on primary consumers) and tertiary consumers (feed on secondary consumers); and Decomposers (saprotrophs, e.g., bacteria and fungi), which break down complex organic matter of dead organisms into simpler inorganic substances, releasing nutrients back to the environment for reuse by producers.
steps: Abiotic components: climatic/edaphic factors, inorganic and organic materials
Biotic components divided into producers, consumers and decomposers
Producers fix CO2 via photosynthesis; consumers (herbivores, carnivores) depend on producers directly/indirectly
Decomposers break down dead organic matter, recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem

question: Define ecological pyramids and describe with examples, pyramids of number and biomass.
solution:
An ecological pyramid is a graphical representation of the trophic structure and function of an ecosystem, starting with producers at the base and successive trophic levels forming the apex, showing the relationship between different trophic levels in terms of number of organisms, biomass, or energy.
Pyramid of numbers: represents the number of individual organisms at each trophic level. It is usually upright in a grassland/pond ecosystem (e.g., a large number of grass plants support fewer herbivores, which support even fewer carnivores), but can be inverted in a tree ecosystem, where a few large trees (producers) support a much larger number of herbivorous insects, which in turn support a smaller number of birds/carnivores.
Pyramid of biomass: represents the total biomass (dry weight or organic matter) present at each trophic level. It is generally upright in most terrestrial ecosystems (e.g., forest, grassland — large producer biomass supporting progressively smaller consumer biomass), but is often inverted in aquatic/pond ecosystems, where the biomass of producers (phytoplankton) at any given time is small compared to the biomass of consumers (zooplankton, fish) they support, since phytoplankton reproduce and are consumed very rapidly.
steps: Ecological pyramid: graphical representation of trophic structure (numbers/biomass/energy) across trophic levels
Pyramid of numbers: usually upright (grassland/pond), but inverted in tree ecosystem (few trees support many insects)
Pyramid of biomass: usually upright (forest/grassland), but often inverted in ponds/aquatic ecosystems (low phytoplankton biomass supports larger consumer biomass)

question: What is primary productivity? Give brief description of factors that affect primary productivity.
solution: Primary productivity is defined as the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants (producers) during photosynthesis. It is expressed in terms of weight (g/m^2/yr) or energy (kcal/m^2/yr). Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total rate of production of organic matter/biomass during photosynthesis, while a considerable amount is utilised by plants in respiration; gross primary productivity minus respiratory losses gives the net primary productivity (NPP), which represents the biomass available for consumption by heterotrophs (herbivores and decomposers). Primary productivity depends on several factors: the plant species inhabiting a particular area (different species/communities have different inherent productive capacities); availability of nutrients in the soil/water; and various environmental/climatic factors such as availability of sunlight, temperature, water/precipitation and carbon dioxide concentration, all of which vary in different types of ecosystems, resulting in different productivity values.
steps: Primary productivity = rate of biomass/organic matter production by producers (photosynthesis) per unit area per time
GPP = total organic matter produced; NPP = GPP minus respiratory losses (available to consumers)
Depends on the plant species/community present, and availability of soil/water nutrients
Also depends on environmental factors: sunlight, temperature, water, and CO2 concentration

question: Define decomposition and describe the processes and products of decomposition.
solution:
Decomposition is the process by which decomposers (mainly bacteria and fungi) break down complex organic matter present in detritus (dead remains of plants/animals and faecal matter) into simpler inorganic substances, which are then released into the soil/environment for reuse by producers.
Processes/steps of decomposition: (i) Fragmentation — detritivores (e.g., earthworms) break down detritus into smaller particles, increasing the surface area for microbial action; (ii) Leaching — water-soluble inorganic nutrients present in the detritus go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts; (iii) Catabolism — bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances through enzymatic breakdown; (iv) Humification — leads to the accumulation of a dark-coloured, amorphous substance called humus, which is highly resistant to microbial action and decomposes very slowly, acting as a reservoir of nutrients; and (v) Mineralisation — humus is further degraded by some microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients (minerals) back into the soil, available for uptake by plant roots.
Products of decomposition include simple inorganic nutrients (such as carbon dioxide, water and mineral nutrients like nitrates, phosphates), and humus, all of which are important for maintaining soil fertility and nutrient cycling in the ecosystem.
steps: Decomposition = breakdown of complex organic (detritus) matter into simpler inorganic substances by decomposers
Fragmentation (by detritivores) increases surface area for microbial action
Leaching, catabolism (enzymatic breakdown), humification (forms resistant humus), and mineralisation (releases inorganic nutrients) are the key processes
Products: CO2, water, mineral nutrients and humus, recycled back into the ecosystem

question: Give an account of energy flow in an ecosystem.
solution: All ecosystems depend on a continuous, unidirectional input of solar energy, of which only about 50% forms photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), and producers (autotrophs) fix only about 2-10% of this PAR through photosynthesis, converting it into chemical (potential) energy stored in food/biomass. This fixed energy then flows from producers to primary consumers (herbivores), then to secondary consumers (carnivores) and so on through successive trophic levels, following a unidirectional path (energy is never recycled, unlike nutrients). At each trophic level, a significant portion of the energy (about 80-90%) is lost as heat during respiration and other metabolic activities, and only about 10% of the energy is transferred/available to the next trophic level (this is known as the ten per cent law, given by Lindeman). This progressive loss of energy at each trophic transfer means the number of trophic levels in a food chain is usually restricted (typically to four or five levels), since the amount of energy available becomes insufficient to support a viable population at higher trophic levels beyond this. Along with this grazing food chain, energy also flows through the detritus food chain, where decomposers break down dead organic matter, releasing energy and nutrients back into the system.
steps: All ecosystems are powered by a unidirectional, continuous input of solar energy (about 50% is PAR)
Producers fix only 2-10% of PAR into chemical energy through photosynthesis
Energy flows unidirectionally from producers through successive trophic levels (herbivores, carnivores)
At each transfer, ~80-90% of energy is lost as heat/respiration, only ~10% passes to the next level (ten per cent law), limiting the number of trophic levels

question: Name the three important components of biodiversity.
solution: The three important components (levels) of biodiversity are: (1) Genetic diversity — variation in genes (DNA sequences) within a single species, occurring across its geographical range, e.g., the numerous varieties of rice, wheat or mango grown in India, or the range of medicinal-compound-producing variants of the Rauwolfia vomitoria plant. (2) Species diversity — the variety/number of species present in a region, e.g., higher species diversity found in the Western Ghats compared to the plains. (3) Ecosystem diversity — the variety of habitats, ecological niches and ecological processes (like nutrient cycling) present, e.g., the diversity of ecosystems in India comprising deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows.
steps: Genetic diversity: variation in genes/DNA within a species (e.g., rice/mango varieties)
Species diversity: variety of species present in a given region
Ecosystem diversity: diversity of habitats and ecological processes across a region
Together these three levels define overall biodiversity

question: How do ecologists estimate the total number of species present in the world?
solution: Since the entire world has not been comprehensively explored for identifying and cataloguing every species, ecologists use indirect statistical methods to estimate the total number of species. One widely used method, pioneered by taxonomist Robert May, involves studying the species richness and number of new species discovered per unit time in a well-explored, species-rich region (like the tropics), and extrapolating that rate of discovery (or the ratio of known to estimated undiscovered species based on patterns from well-studied groups) globally, particularly to less-studied taxonomic groups and geographic regions (like tropical forests), to arrive at an overall global estimate of species richness (commonly cited estimates range around 7 million species).
steps: Not all regions of the world/taxonomic groups have been fully explored/catalogued
Ecologists use extrapolation methods based on species discovery rates in well-studied regions (e.g., tropics)
This method (associated with Robert May) projects known patterns to under-explored groups/regions
Gives an estimated total global species count (commonly cited as around 7 million)

question: Give three hypotheses for explaining why tropics show greatest levels of species richness.
solution:
Three hypotheses explaining greater species richness in the tropics are:
1. Speciation is generally a function of time; tropical regions have remained relatively undisturbed for millions of years (unlike temperate regions, which suffered periodic glaciations), allowing a much longer evolutionary time for species diversification to occur.
2. Tropical environments, unlike temperate ones, are less seasonal, relatively more constant and predictable, and this environmental stability promotes niche specialisation and leads to a greater degree of species diversity.
